title: As electric two-wheelers gain a foothold, Belgian startup Any bets on cargo space
slides: Can a cargo e-bike really replace a van?
Belgian startup Any thinks so, with modular boxes.
Most cargo bikes fail on last-mile delivery costs.
Any's swap system cuts loading time dramatically.
Test one route against your van this month.
thread_text:
1. Vans are losing.

Any's modular cargo e-bike system swaps boxes in seconds, cutting loading time so much that last-mile delivery costs finally drop below van thresholds.

2. The real problem.

Most cargo bikes fail because loading and unloading eats the savings. Any's boxes attack that exact bottleneck, not the pedaling.

3. Swap, don't load.

Instead of filling a bike box item by item, drivers swap pre-filled modules. It's the same idea as changing a battery, but for freight.

4. Route test this month.

Any is challenging delivery firms to run one real route with their e-bike against a van. Concrete numbers, not marketing promises.

5. Will you test it?

If you manage last-mile deliveries, ask Any for a demo on your hardest route. Measure time and cost per stop. See if it beats your van.

instagram.caption:
Vans spend most of their last-mile delivery time parked, while drivers load and unload boxes item by item. 🚐

Belgian startup Any is betting a modular cargo e-bike can replace them—with boxes that swap in seconds, like changing a battery for freight. Most cargo bikes fail on cost because loading eats the savings; this attack fixes that bottleneck, not the pedaling. 📦

For delivery managers, that means a concrete route test this month: run one real route against your van, measure time and cost per stop.

Will you put your hardest delivery route on an e-bike against your van before the end of March? ⏱️
